How to fill it in

What this template is, and is not

This is a structure and a worked example. The company name, people, figures and story are invented. The title slide says so, and the placeholder company is called [Your Company]. Replace every slide with your own facts before you send it to anyone. Do not leave any sample number in a deck you send to investors.

Step 1: Start with the ask

Before you edit slide 1, write one sentence for slide 13: how much you are raising, what you will do with it and what milestone it reaches. Everything else in the deck exists to make that sentence believable. Edit the amount, the round and the use-of-funds percentages, and make sure they add up to 100%. Change the milestones to ones you can really hit.

Step 2: Problem, solution and why now

Slide 2: write three pains your buyer has, in their words, and one hard number with a source. If you cannot source a statistic, delete it rather than keep a guess. Slide 3: say what changes for the buyer when they use you, in one sentence and three pillars. Slide 4: list three dated shifts (regulation, technology, behaviour) that make this possible now. Keep titles to two lines and bullets to about 15 words.

Step 3: Size the market from the bottom up

On slide 5, replace the sample figures with the number of accounts you can reach and the annual price you charge. TAM is all such accounts times your price; SAM is the part you can serve with your product and channels; SOM is what you can win in a few years. Show the arithmetic, because investors check it. Avoid “if we get 1% of a $50 billion market”.

Step 4: Edit the charts with real data

On the traction slide, click the chart, choose Chart Design > Edit Data and type in your own monthly figures. The sample shows revenue growing for twelve months; yours may be flatter, and that is fine if the slide title says what is true. For the financial summary, replace the projection with your model’s outputs and be ready to defend every year. If you do not have a model yet, see the Excel financial model guide.

Step 5: Business model, competition, go-to-market, team

Slide 8: your pricing tiers and unit economics (CAC, payback, retention). Use only figures you have measured or label them as targets. Slide 9: pick five capabilities your buyer cares about and score yourself and two or three alternatives honestly; investors distrust a grid where you win every row. Slide 10: three phases of how you will find customers, with the metric for each. Slide 11: for each founder, one line about why they are the right person for this problem.

Step 6: Check it before you send

Read every slide title in order; they should tell the whole story on their own. Check that the same number is the same everywhere (revenue, raise, runway). Remove the sample notice and speaker notes you do not want investors to see. Export a PDF for emailing and keep the PowerPoint for presenting. For more on structure, see the pitch deck guide.

Frequently asked questions

Is this pitch deck template really free?

Yes. Download the .pptx without signing up and use it for your own fundraising.

Do the charts work in PowerPoint?

Yes. They are native PowerPoint charts. Right-click and Edit Data to change the numbers. Keynote and Google Slides can open the file, but chart editing there can differ.

Are the numbers real?

No. The company, people and every figure are fictional samples. Replace them all.

Is it for seed or Series A?

The structure works for both. Seed decks lean on the problem and the team; Series A decks lean on traction and unit economics.

How many slides should a pitch deck have?

Thirteen is a sensible starting point for a deck you send. Many founders keep an extra appendix for detail.
